title: China's Workers Now Support More Elderly than Children
paragraphs: For the first time, China's working-age population is supporting more elderly people than children, according to official data released at the end of October.

The figures concern what are known as dependency ratios. These compare the number of people who are considered too young or too old to work with the number of people of working age, defined as those between 15 and 64. In 2025, China's old-age dependency ratio, which measures people aged 65 and over, reached 23.1%. Meanwhile, its child dependency ratio, which measures children aged 14 and under, stood at 22%.
In other words, there are now more than 223 million people aged 65 or older in China, compared with roughly 213 million children.

This shift has been coming for years. The old-age dependency ratio has risen steadily, from 15% in 2016 to 20.8% in 2021 and 22.8% in 2024. At the same time, the number of births has fallen sharply. China's population declined in 2025 for the fourth year in a row, while the birth rate dropped to a record low.

The Chinese government has attempted to reverse the trend. After decades of strict limits on family size, it began allowing couples to have two children in 2016, and then raised the limit to three children in 2021. However, these changes have not led to a significant rise in births. Many young couples say they are choosing to have fewer children, or none at all, because of the high cost of housing, education and childcare.

An aging population creates serious economic challenges for any country. As the number of older people grows, the country will need to spend more on pensions and health care. At the same time, a shrinking workforce means fewer people paying taxes and contributing to economic growth.

It is worth noting, however, that the dependency ratio does not count how many people actually have jobs. It simply compares age groups, so the real economic burden on workers depends on how many working-age people are employed.
